outline: Hypoglycemia secondary to surreptitious insulin use
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Endogenous pancreatic beta cells synthesize proinsulin and cleave it into insulin and C-peptide before secretion. Exogenous insulin provides insulin without accompanying C-peptide or proinsulin. Therefore, during hypoglycemia caused by exogenous insulin, circulating insulin is inappropriately elevated while endogenous C-peptide and proinsulin are suppressed. Insulin secretagogues and insulinoma instead stimulate endogenous insulin secretion and therefore raise C-peptide; a secretagogue screen helps distinguish medication ingestion from insulinoma.
vignette: A 32-year-old woman without diabetes is evaluated for recurrent episodes of diaphoresis, tremor, confusion, and near-syncope that improve promptly after she consumes glucose. During a supervised symptomatic episode, plasma glucose is low. At the same time, plasma insulin is inappropriately elevated, whereas C-peptide and proinsulin are suppressed. A serum screen for sulfonylureas and meglitinides is negative. Liver and kidney function are normal, and she has no hyperpigmentation or electrolyte abnormalities.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypoglycemia?
distractor_notes: Insulinoma causes endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Because insulin and C-peptide are co-secreted by pancreatic beta cells, insulinoma is associated with inappropriately elevated insulin together with elevated C-peptide and proinsulin during hypoglycemia, not suppression of C-peptide and proinsulin.

Sulfonylureas and other insulin secretagogues stimulate pancreatic insulin release, producing elevated insulin together with elevated C-peptide. Detection of the drug in blood or urine distinguishes secretagogue exposure from insulinoma; this patient's secretagogue screen is negative and C-peptide is suppressed.

Some non-islet-cell tumors cause hypoglycemia through excess IGF-2 signaling. Endotext notes that insulin and C-peptide are appropriately suppressed during this form of hypoglycemia, so it does not match the inappropriately elevated insulin level in this patient.

Cortisol deficiency can impair the counterregulatory response to hypoglycemia, but primary adrenal insufficiency does not produce the distinctive combination of elevated insulin with suppressed C-peptide and proinsulin. Typical associated findings can include hyperpigmentation and electrolyte abnormalities, which are absent here.
key_expl: This biochemical pattern indicates exogenous insulin exposure. Insulin and C-peptide are produced together when endogenous pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin. In contrast, injected insulin contains no C-peptide; therefore, exogenous insulin–induced hypoglycemia produces inappropriately high insulin with suppressed C-peptide and proinsulin. Insulinoma and sulfonylurea exposure both stimulate endogenous insulin secretion and therefore do not fit the suppressed C-peptide pattern; a negative secretagogue screen additionally argues against sulfonylurea or meglitinide ingestion.
objective: Differentiate causes of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia using insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, and insulin-secretagogue testing: elevated insulin with suppressed C-peptide/proinsulin indicates exogenous insulin administration.

sources.title: Factitious Hypoglycemia
sources.date: StatPearls in NCBI Bookshelf; 2026 edition; verified 2026-08-28
sources.support: NCBI states that exogenous insulin causes elevated plasma insulin with suppressed C-peptide and proinsulin, whereas insulinoma and insulin secretagogues cause elevation of insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin; secretagogue detection distinguishes medication-induced hypoglycemia from insulinoma.

sources.title: Non-Diabetic Hypoglycemia — Endotext
sources.locator: Fasting Hypoglycemia; Factitial Hypoglycemia; Non-Islet Cell Tumors; Addison's Disease
sources.support: Endotext describes exogenous insulin hypoglycemia as elevated insulin with suppressed C-peptide; secretagogue hypoglycemia as elevated insulin and C-peptide; IGF-2 non-islet-cell tumor hypoglycemia as appropriately suppressed insulin and C-peptide; and adrenal insufficiency as a non-hyperinsulinemic cause associated with cortisol deficiency.

sources.title: Biochemistry, C Peptide
sources.support: NCBI explains that C-peptide is elevated with endogenous beta-cell insulin secretion such as insulinoma or sulfonylurea exposure and decreased with factitious exogenous insulin administration.
